<reason>Both sides were competent and grounded, but CON controlled the clash's trajectory. PRO's opening analogy (digital library = bookshelf) was effectively dismantled by the rivalry argument, forcing PRO into the "one seat" concession, which CON then exploited twice: first as unsplittable (two of three heirs get nothing), then as unsaleable (probate divides value only through markets, and a non-transferable seat has none). CON's pressure question on "next of kin" vs "estate's designee" exposed a real tension; PRO's intestacy-default answer was plausible and honest, but CON never had to concede it because CON's deeper line—the statutory guarantee delivers only a promise on a mortal platform, "a receipt for a promise"—survived PRO's counterparty-risk analogy and directly attacked the motion's own word "guarantee." PRO's best late move (CON's DRM-free remedy is a bigger intervention that abandons existing purchasers) was a genuine crystallization, but CON's reply that both legislate against the license and only one leaves the buyer something splittable, saleable, and seller-independent was cleaner. PRO also bore two clipped turns (opening and rebuttal 2), an execution cost, plus mild internal tension between "single-user terms carry forward" and later suggesting a market for seats. CON generated fresh, adaptive pressure every round and made the debate easier to decide.</best_rebuttal>
<best_rebuttal>Side B's second rebuttal (B4): answering PRO's pressure questions, B reframed its remedy as changing the *thing* (rivalrous DRM-free file, hence already chattel-like) rather than the *timing*, then delivered the decisive distinction that probate divides indivisible assets by *selling* them and a non-transferable seat has no market—turning PRO's own "unsplittable" question into the "unsaleable" objection PRO never fully resolved.</best_rebuttal>
